name: Fillout
tagline: Build a polished form that writes to a user-owned database and supports simple branching

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Unlimited forms, seats, questions and file uploads; 1,000 responses/month; 20MB maximum file size; Fillout branding

tiers.name: Starter
tiers.limits: 2,000 responses/month and 20MB maximum file size; unlimited forms, seats, questions and uploads
tiers.notes: Annual price is $180/year; monthly total is $228/year at $19/month.

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: Unlimited responses, at least 1GB maximum file size, custom domain, unlimited forms and seats

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: 1 million+ database records, unlimited workflow runs, unlimited forms, seats and responses

pricing.freeTierCaps: Unlimited forms, seats, questions and file uploads; 1,000 responses/month; 20MB maximum file size; Fillout branding
pricing.hiddenCosts: Fillout says responses continue to be collected after the monthly cap, but the account must upgrade, buy unpublished bulk-submission capacity or wait for reset to use them; Conversion Kit is a separately sold add-on with no public rate.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For Fillout, build a polished form that writes to a user-owned database and supports simple branching. The hard boundary is excellent airtable and notion integrations, scheduling, payments, and hosted polish, plus integrations, deliverability, and workflow depth.
coreLoopDIY: Build a public form that writes to a user-owned database and supports simple branching, validate submissions, notify the owner, and provide a private response table with CSV export.
requirements: Resend API key or SMTP credentials
whatYouLose: excellent Airtable and Notion integrations, scheduling, payments, and hosted polish
ongoingBurden: spam control, email delivery, storage, exports, accessibility, conditional logic, and integrations
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Fillout because a basic form is trivial; people pay when the form feeds a dependable business workflow and never loses a response. The recurring cost buys spam control, email delivery, storage, exports, accessibility, conditional logic, and integrations, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Formbricks
priorArt.desc: Active open-source survey and experience-management platform.

alternatives.name: Baserow
alternatives.desc: Airtable's database half with public forms and your own disk underneath

rejectedAlternatives.name: Grist
rejectedAlternatives.desc: It owns the database, but conditional questions remain an open feature request

rejectedAlternatives.name: NocoDB
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The Community edition writes to your database, but conditional fields, validation, and redirects are paid

rejectedAlternatives.name: Teable
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Basic forms lack branching; Teable points you to its advanced App Builder for conditional multi-step flows

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Starter plan and a single-owner form service DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Fillout in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, SQLite, Drizzle ORM, and Resend; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: build a public form that writes to a user-owned database and supports simple branching, validate submissions, notify the owner, and provide a private response table with CSV export.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create a form builder with short text, long text, email, number, select, radio, checkbox, and file fields.
Publish each form at a stable slug with server-side validation and accessible labels.
Add honeypot, rate limiting, submission-size limits, and a clear privacy notice.
Store responses in SQLite and provide search, filters, detail view, and CSV export.
Send an owner notification without placing submitted values in logs.
Support a thank-you screen and one simple conditional branch.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out payment collection.
Deliberately leave out hundreds of third-party integrations.
Deliberately leave out multi-brand enterprise workspaces and compliance attestations.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
